Either clear the target on every row this session may score before calling fit(), or use predict(), which excludes the rows it scores from the context it sends.

This client accepts it and says how many rows the model will not see

{where} is the time column and is written two ways: {year_first!r} leads with its year and {other!r} leads with its day or its month. No one reading covers both. The call that reads {other!r} reads {year_first!r} as a different date, so read the halves apart and put them back as one column, or store frame[{column!r}] in one shape before naming it as the time column.{also}

{where} is the time column and holds text such as {example!r}, which does not say unambiguously what date it is: read day-first it is one date and month-first another, and nothing in the column says which. Convert it yourself so the reading is yours: frame[{column!r}] = pd.to_datetime(frame[{column!r}], dayfirst=True), or store it year-first

Say how {'they join' if many else 'it joins'}: schema.relationships.append(Relationship({unlinked[0]!r}, <foreign key>, <parent table>, <its primary key>)), or leave {'them' if many else 'it'} out of the schema to say {'they are' if many else 'it is'} not wanted.

{', '.join((repr(name) for name in unreached))} {'are' if many else 'is'} linked into the schema and not in this request: the sampler reached no row of {'them' if many else 'it'} from the entities being scored, so the model answers without {'them' if many else 'it'}. Raise num_hops if {'they lie' if many else 'it lies'} further out than the hops sampled, and check the foreign key holds values the parent key actually has if {'they do' if many else 'it does'} not.

{', '.join((str(link) for link in empty))} {'join' if many else 'joins'} none of the rows given: no value of the foreign key appears in the key it points at, so the tables are related in the schema and in no row of the data, and the question is answered as though {'they' if many else 'it'} were not declared. Check that the foreign key is the column naming the parent row; one spelled differently from the key it points at has to be said outright, as relationships=[Relationship({first.source_table!r}, <that column>, {first.target_table!r}, {first.target_column!r})].

{', '.join(ignored)} {'are' if many else 'is'} typed {' or '.join(sorted(unread))}, which this model does not read, so the request is answered without {'them' if many else 'it'} and {'they contribute' if many else 'it contributes'} nothing to the prediction. Type a column categorical if its values are labels rather than prose, or leave it out to say so.

{key!r} is the primary key of {_and_list(shared)}, so a column named {key!r} identifies a row in each of them and names a parent in none. No relationship is inferred through an ambiguous name, so nothing can point at any of those tables: none of them is gathered as another table's related rows, and a question about one of them is answered from that table alone. Say what the graph is: relationships=[Relationship(child, column, {shared[0]!r}, {key!r}), ...], or give each table a key of its own name, so that the column naming it can be matched to it.

{source!r} and {target!r} name each other, and a relationship is crossed in both directions, so this is two ways over one pair and an aggregation between them is refused for not having a single one. Declare whichever of the two a question is about and leave the other out.

{source!r} reaches {target!r} through {_and_list(sorted(columns))}, and an aggregation across the two tables has to be resolved to one of them, so a query that crosses this pair is refused until it is. They are all kept because they are all real, and which one a question means is not something this can decide. To keep {kept!r}, drop the others: schema.relationships = [link for link in schema.relationships if not (link.source_table == {source!r} and link.target_table == {target!r} and link.source_column in {sorted(rest)!r})].
